title: RBI Open to More Steps to Defend Rupee and Curb Forex Speculation, Governor Malhotra Says
excerpt: Governor Sanjay Malhotra told Moneycontrol the central bank's recent curbs target speculative derivatives trading, not genuine hedging, and should not be read as capital controls. The rupee outperformed Asian peers after the measures.
body:
• RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the central bank would consider further measures, if needed, to curb speculative trading in the forex market.
  • The RBI has extended curbs on certain derivative transactions, opened a special dollar window for oil firms, and intervened aggressively as the rupee slipped toward record lows.
  • The rupee rose as much as 0.8% to 95.01 per dollar in the previous session after a 1% gain on Monday; offshore non-deliverable forwards eased to 95.36 on Wednesday.
  • For NRIs sending money home, the RBI-supported level near 95 per dollar — not the record lows threatened last week — is the rate remittances are currently converting at.

The Reserve Bank of India would consider further measures, if needed, to curb speculative trading in the foreign exchange market, Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in an interview to Moneycontrol, reported by NDTV. "The RBI is determined to do whatever is necessary to ensure orderly movement in the foreign exchange market," Malhotra said late Tuesday.

He said the central bank's recent steps should not be seen as capital control measures, and were aimed at ensuring forex markets serve genuine hedging needs rather than speculative bets.

What the RBI has already done

The extended curbs added to steps taken over the weekend, including a special window for oil firms to meet their dollar demand and broader restrictions on derivatives markets as the rupee slipped toward record lows. The central bank has also been intervening aggressively in the currency market to defend the local unit.

Malhotra pointed to the pattern the curbs target: over the past few months, the RBI observed a very high proportion of trades being cancelled and rebooked on the same day — in some cases about one-third of trades were closed or cancelled on the day they were entered into.

The market response so far has favoured the central bank. The rupee edged higher in the offshore market on Wednesday, with dollar-rupee non-deliverable forwards easing as much as 0.1% to 95.36. The currency outperformed Asian peers in the previous session, rising as much as 0.8% to 95.01 per dollar, following Monday's 1% gain.

Rates are part of the defence

Earlier this month, the RBI's monetary policy committee raised its benchmark repurchase rate by 25 basis points to contain accelerating inflation and support the weakening rupee amid a foreign fund selloff. Malhotra said the external sector was India's main macroeconomic challenge despite robust domestic growth, healthy bank balance sheets and improving corporate earnings, and that the central bank is watching geopolitical headwinds closely. Price stability, he said, cannot be achieved without financial stability, because a stable financial system is essential for monetary policy transmission.

"I believe forex markets are getting unduly pessimistic about the Indian economy's future, which is actually underpinned by strong economic fundamentals."

— Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India

The official line is coordinated

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Tuesday at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi that the RBI will continue its efforts to curb volatility in the rupee — the same forum at which, as we report separately, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said the India-US trade deal is nearing a landing point, an outcome that would remove one of the largest external pressures on the currency.

What to watch

Whether the RBI follows through with additional curbs, and whether foreign fund flows stabilise, will decide if 95 per dollar holds. For remitters, moves of 1% in a week — the scale seen since Monday — change the rupee value of a $1,000 transfer by roughly Rs 950, so timing transfers around RBI intervention days has a measurable payoff.
